passage:
Tuesday. Manoj called Dhruv an hour before the cricket match. "So you'd rather play than help me with my project? Fine. I'll do it alone, like always. Nobody cares." Dhruv felt his stomach drop and stayed home.
The next Monday. Same pattern: Manoj sighed loudly in the canteen about being abandoned until Dhruv gave up his lunch hour to sit with him. Afterwards Dhruv realised he could not remember the last time he had said no and been forgiven quickly.
Friday. "I can help on Saturday morning for two hours," Dhruv said. "I can't drop everything every time." Manoj went silent, then said, "Real friends would do more." Dhruv's hands were shaky, but he said, "I'm still here for those two hours." On Sunday a meme arrived from Manoj.

qa.q: How long did Dhruv offer to help on Saturday morning?
qa.a: He offered to help for two hours.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv's stomach drop when Manoj called before the match?
qa.a: He felt guilty and afraid of letting a friend down, because Manoj framed the choice as Dhruv not caring. That is why he gave up the match.

qa.q: What could Dhruv try if Manoj keeps using guilt?
qa.a: He can keep naming what he will and will not do, like the two hours, and repeat it calmly. Friends who respect him will accept a no.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Dhruv's new limit?
qa.a: Manoj may feel hurt or worried about losing the support he is used to, which could explain the line about real friends. The meme on Sunday suggests he did not want to end things.

grounding: A friend uses guilt and drama to keep the protagonist close, and he starts naming what he will and will not do.

subtype: Friend × Recognising a toxic pattern from outside [Actor]
passage:
Dear Ramesh,
I have been thinking about how to say this, so I will say it once and then leave it. Over the last few months you have stopped coming to cricket, you check your phone before answering me, and last week you looked frightened when a call came in. I might be wrong. I am not telling you what to do, and I am not asking you to choose between us. I just want you to know what I have noticed, and that I am on your side either way. I will keep saving your seat in the canteen. If you want to talk, or just sit quietly, call me any time, day or night, and I will not ask questions.
Your friend,
Jatin

qa.q: What has Jatin noticed about Ramesh over the last few months?
qa.a: Jatin noticed that Ramesh stopped coming to cricket, checks the phone before answering, and looked frightened when a call came in.

qa.q: What is Jatin worried about, and how can you tell from the careful wording?
qa.a: Jatin worries about Ramesh but does not want Ramesh to feel judged or cornered. Writing "I might be wrong" and "I am not asking you to choose" shows care for the friendship and a wish to keep the door open.

qa.q: What could Jatin do after sending the letter?
qa.a: Jatin can keep the seat saved, stay in touch in ordinary ways, listen without judging, and not repeat the warning or give ultimatums.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Ramesh may feel worried, exposed or defensive at first, but also relieved that there is no pressure. Ramesh also learns someone is ready to listen at any hour.

grounding: A friend sees a controlling relationship from outside, shares the concern once, and keeps the door open without ultimatums.

passage: Shalini's acceptance letter for the design course in another city lay open on the dining table. Kavitha Masi read it twice and put her spectacles down. "I brought you up after your mother's illness. I gave up my job for you. But go, go. Don't worry about an old woman eating dinner alone." Shalini felt the familiar tug, like a rope round her chest. Old Shalini would have said, "I'll stay, Masi," and resented it for years. She took a breath. "Masi, I know what you gave up, and I love you for it. I am still going. I will call every evening and come home for the holidays." Kavitha Masi's eyes were wet, but she nodded, and pushed the plate of dosas towards her.

qa.q: What was lying open on the dining table?
qa.a: Shalini's acceptance letter for the design course in another city was lying open.

qa.q: What did the rope round her chest tell us about how Shalini felt?
qa.a: It shows Shalini felt pulled by guilt and love at once, and expected she might give in and resent it later.

qa.q: What could Shalini do to keep the bond strong while still going?
qa.a: She can keep her promises to call every evening and visit on holidays, and keep acknowledging what her aunt gave without changing her decision. 🙂

qa.q: How might Kavitha Masi be feeling?
qa.a: Kavitha Masi is probably afraid of being lonely and hurt to see Shalini leave. Her wet eyes and the plate of dosas show she still loves her and accepts the choice.

grounding: A relative uses guilt and sacrifice to steer the protagonist's choice; she acknowledges the love and still chooses for herself.

subtype: Cult or group × Love and belonging with control [Receiver]
passage:
Dear Lokesh bhaiya,
I am writing because you are the only one who will not laugh. Since August I have been going to the evening circle at the hostel. They call me family, they remember my birthday, they even wrote me a poem. It felt like coming home. But I have started noticing things. We are told not to tell our parents what is said inside. The leader says part of my stipend should go to "the work", and when I asked where it goes, he said doubt is a lack of faith. I miss how warm the first weeks felt. That is why I am telling you. I am going home this weekend, and I want to talk to Papa. Please call me on Sunday.
Shankar

qa.q: Since when has Shankar been going to the evening circle?
qa.a: Shankar has been going since August.

qa.q: Why does Shankar say he misses how warm the first weeks felt?
qa.a: He felt real belonging at first, and he is torn because that warmth was what drew him in, even though he now sees signs of control.

qa.q: What signs in the group could Shankar check further?
qa.a: He can check whether he is allowed to question, whether he can leave freely, whether they demand secrecy or money, and keep his ties with his family and outside friends.

qa.q: How might Lokesh bhaiya feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lokesh bhaiya may feel worried but also trusted, since Shankar says he is the only one who will not laugh. The Sunday call gives him a way to stay close.

grounding: A friendly group offers belonging but demands secrecy, money and obedience; the protagonist notices he cannot question it and keeps his family ties.

passage: The corridor outside the viva room was loud with first-years, and Vijay had ten minutes to spare when Sarita caught his sleeve. "Vijay bhaiya, you never fail at anything! How do you do it?" Two other juniors leaned in, waiting. He could feel how nice it would be to just nod. Instead he laughed and said, "I failed two papers in my first year. I nearly quit. I sat in the library for a whole month with a friend who explained things to me." Sarita blinked. "Really?" "Really. Don't put me on a shelf, I fall off it." He glanced at the clock, waved, and went in for his viva, a little nervous, and glad he had said it.

qa.q: What did Sarita ask Vijay in the corridor?
qa.a: She asked how he never failed at anything.

qa.q: What did Vijay feel as the juniors leaned in, and what did he decide?
qa.a: He felt how nice it would be to just nod and be admired, but he chose to be honest about his failures instead.

qa.q: What could Vijay do to keep the juniors' admiration healthy?
qa.a: He can keep sharing honest stories about setbacks and what helped him, and avoid using their admiration to get favours.

qa.q: How might Sarita see Vijay after his answer?
qa.a: Sarita may be surprised but also encouraged, since she learns that even someone she looks up to failed and recovered. Her "Really?" shows her picture of him shifting.

grounding: Juniors treat the protagonist as perfect; he stays honest about his flaws and does not let it inflate him.

passage: Honestly, I was a bit of a copy machine last year. Tarun bhaiya was our senior in the debate club, and I thought he was flawless. I copied his haircut, his way of clearing his throat before speaking, even the phrases he used. My roommate said, "Who are you?" and I laughed it off. Then in one meeting Tarun bhaiya argued for something I disagreed with, and I clapped anyway, because that is what I did. Walking back, I realised I had not formed a thought of my own in months. It scared me a little. Now I still watch how he prepares and how patiently he listens, and I take that. But what I say in the debate hall, I decide. I am Nilesh again, and I like him better.

qa.q: What club was Tarun in when Nilesh admired him?
qa.a: Tarun was a senior in the debate club.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh feel scared after clapping for something he disagreed with?
qa.a: He realised he had not formed a thought of his own in months, and feared he was losing himself in copying someone else.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do to keep learning from seniors without copying?
qa.a: He can learn qualities like Tarun's preparation and patient listening, and test each opinion against his own judgement before he speaks or claps. 😊

qa.q: How might Nilesh's roommate have seen the copying?
qa.a: The roommate saw a friend becoming unfamiliar, hence "Who are you?", and may have been worried or puzzled. Nilesh laughed it off then, but it stayed in his mind.

grounding: A junior copies a senior's every move, then learns their qualities while keeping his own judgement.

passage: Every time Rukmini spoke in the marketing meeting, Aparna looked at the ceiling. In the pantry she turned her back. Nobody at the firm could say why. Rukmini spent a week bringing her tea, offering to share notes, laughing a bit too hard at Aparna's jokes. Nothing changed. On Friday evening, walking to the metro, she asked herself just once: had she ever taken credit that was Aparna's, or spoken sharply? She went through the months slowly and found nothing. It stung. But she made herself stop. Monday she said a normal good morning, and when Aparna did not answer, she simply went to her desk. She did not complain to anyone or hint at anything. Her lunch with two other colleagues was easier than it had been in weeks.

qa.q: What did Aparna do whenever Rukmini spoke in the meeting?
qa.a: Aparna looked at the ceiling.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini keep offering tea and notes for a week?
qa.a: She wanted Aparna's approval and hoped kindness would end the dislike. It hurt when nothing changed.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do if Aparna's coldness continues?
qa.a: She can keep being polite and professional, keep her good relationships with others, and speak to a supervisor only if it starts affecting her work.

qa.q: How might Aparna see Rukmini's changed behaviour on Monday?
qa.a: Aparna may notice that Rukmini has stopped trying so hard and simply says good morning. The passage does not say what Aparna thinks or why she dislikes her.

grounding: A peer openly dislikes the protagonist for no clear reason; she reflects once, then stops chasing approval without retaliating.

passage:
Ankita: Saw Meher's post again. Her big internship. So smug 😒
Jyoti: You mention her ten times a day. What did she actually do to you?
Ankita: Nothing. That's what's so annoying. I just can't stand her.
Jyoti: Then why can't you stop looking?
Ankita: ...because she got the internship I wanted?
Ankita: I keep rehearsing things I'd say to her. I nearly told people she cheated. I've no proof.
Jyoti: That sounds more like hurt than hatred. Please don't say that to anyone.
Ankita: I know. I know. 😔
Jyoti: Mute her for a week? Chai at six?
Ankita: Okay. Chai.

qa.q: What post of Meher's did Ankita see?
qa.a: Ankita saw Meher's post about her big internship.

qa.q: What does Ankita realise about her feelings towards Meher?
qa.a: She realises her dislike is tied to envy and hurt over the internship she wanted, not to anything Meher did to her.

qa.q: What could Ankita do to loosen her hold on this?
qa.a: She can mute Meher for a while, not spread the cheating rumour, and put the energy into her own applications, with Jyoti's support. 🙂

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Ankita's anger?
qa.a: Jyoti sees it as hurt more than hatred and gently asks questions instead of judging. Jyoti also asks Ankita not to share the cheating claim with anyone.

grounding: The protagonist dislikes someone deeply and cannot stop thinking of them, then sees the envy and old hurt behind it and steps away.

subtype: Online group × Being trolled or shamed [Receiver]
passage: The night before his thermodynamics exam, Joseph's post about a film had gone the wrong way. Strangers mocked his accent, called him names, and their comments were still arriving. His hands shook over the keyboard. He typed a long reply, and Reena, from the next bunk, looked over. "Don't send that." "They're lying about me!" "They'll only get more to pile on." She showed him how to screenshot the worst messages, block the accounts, and switch off notifications until tomorrow. Joseph felt hot behind his eyes. "It hurts, though." "I know. It says nothing true about you." She made two cups of tea, and they went through his formulas until midnight. In the morning, he still felt bruised, but he walked into the exam.

qa.q: What did Reena tell Joseph not to do?
qa.a: She told him not to send his long reply.

qa.q: What was Joseph feeling as he typed his long reply?
qa.a: He was angry and hurt, and wanted to defend himself against people he felt were lying about him. His shaking hands and hot eyes show it.

qa.q: What steps could Joseph take if the comments continue?
qa.a: He can keep his screenshots as evidence, keep the accounts blocked, avoid replying, and report the abuse to the platform and, if it continues, to a trusted adult or the college.

qa.q: How does Reena see the trolling?
qa.a: Reena sees it as something that says nothing true about Joseph. She helps him step away and studies with him.

grounding: Strangers pile on over a post; the protagonist does not engage, saves evidence, blocks, and leans on a real friend.

passage: In the computer lab, Aparna noticed that when she sat down, the two rows nearby went quiet. Her marks had topped the last three tests, and Akash, who had been friendly in first year, now only said, "Must be nice." She felt the sting. For a moment she thought of failing a test on purpose, or hiding her answers, so it would stop. Then she remembered how much she loved the subject. At the next lab, when Akash's program crashed, she said, "Want me to look? I got stuck on the same thing last week." He hesitated, then shifted his chair. She did not mention her marks or her rank. The rows around them stayed quiet, but Akash stopped looking away when she walked in.

qa.q: What did Akash say to Aparna about her marks?
qa.a: He said, "Must be nice."

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when the nearby rows went quiet, and what did she consider doing?
qa.a: She felt the sting of being treated coldly, and briefly considered hiding her ability. She then decided against it because she loved the subject.

qa.q: What could Aparna do if the coldness continues?
qa.a: She can stay kind, help when asked, avoid flaunting her marks, and keep enjoying her work. If it becomes bullying she can tell a teacher.

qa.q: How might Akash see Aparna's offer to look at his program?
qa.a: Akash may have felt envy or discomfort, and he hesitated. Her plain offer, without any mention of marks, seems to have made it easier for him to accept.

grounding: People treat the protagonist coldly because of her marks; she stays kind, does not flaunt, and does not hide her gifts.
